q: CS13: An empty token bucket refills at 2 tokens/s. A request arrives 250 ms after the last update. How much longer until one token is available?
options: 250 ms
500 ms
750 ms
explanation: The bucket has refilled 0.5 token in 250 ms. The remaining 0.5 token needs another 250 ms. An integer-seconds Retry-After header rounds that remaining wait up to one second.

q: CS13: Eight gateways each receive three independent emergency tokens with no refill and no reset on restart. What additional admission bound follows for one outage epoch?
options: At most 3 extra requests
At most 24 extra requests
At most 8 extra requests
At most 11 extra requests
explanation: Each of eight gateways can spend three extra tokens, so the total extra budget is 24. This is not a percentage guarantee and fails if restarts replenish the emergency budget.

q: CS13: A compliance endpoint must accept at most 100 requests in every rolling 60-second interval. Which mechanism directly matches this requirement?
options: A full 100-token bucket refilling at 100/minute
A fixed-minute counter reset at each minute boundary
An atomic log of accepted timestamps in the last 60 seconds
Independent 100/minute counters at each gateway
explanation: A sliding-window log counts the accepted requests in the exact rolling interval. A token bucket allows burst plus refill, a fixed window has boundary effects, and independent gateways multiply the allowance.

q: CS13: Redis server time moves backward from stored timestamp 1200 ms to 1190 ms. Which refill rule avoids both negative refill and later counting the interval twice?
options: Use the gateway clock and overwrite the stored timestamp
Subtract ten milliseconds of tokens and store 1190 ms
Refill by the absolute time difference and store 1190 ms
Use max(server time, stored time) and retain 1200 ms
explanation: Clamping effective time to the previous timestamp adds no refill during the backward step and does not replay the elapsed interval later. Server TIME is authoritative wall time, not inherently monotonic.

q: CS13: A central bucket deducts ten tokens before granting them to gateway G. G spends four and crashes. What is the safe interpretation of the remaining grant?
options: Six tokens may be stranded until the grant is safely invalidated
Six tokens can immediately be issued to every other gateway
The central bucket must undo all ten spent and unspent tokens
The crash proves G can never resume and spend its remaining six
explanation: Pre-deducted grants avoid inventing capacity, but unused grants may be stranded. Reissuing tokens while an old process can still spend them breaks the global bound; safe invalidation or expiry is needed.

q: CS13: A Redis replica is promoted after losing recent acknowledged token spends. What can the limiter truthfully claim?
options: Lua atomicity preserves the old global bound across this loss
The promotion can over-admit unless the durability contract prevents it
Using server time reconstructs the exact number of lost token spends
Adding a Retry-After header restores the missing bucket history
explanation: Lua prevents interleaving on one owner, not loss of acknowledged state during asynchronous failover. Strict admission guarantees need a suitable durability/ownership protocol or must stop admitting during uncertainty.

q: CS14: An ID uses 41 timestamp bits, 10 worker bits and 12 sequence bits. Which expression extracts the worker field from a nonnegative ID?
explanation: Shift away the 12 sequence bits, then mask the next 10 bits with 1023. Shifting by 22 extracts the timestamp offset, while masking with 4095 extracts the sequence.

q: CS14: Worker 7's old process last reported offset 1040, but its durable timestamp grant ends at 1100. Which earliest replacement offset is safe under the chapter's non-overlapping grant scheme?
options: 1040 with sequence reset to zero
1041 with sequence reset to zero
1100 with a new lease generation
1101 after wall time reaches it
explanation: The old allocation may have issued any timestamp through 1100. The replacement starts strictly above the durable ceiling, not merely above the last reported ID. An unencoded lease generation does not change the ID tuple.

q: CS14: A generator cannot renew its worker lease and reaches its conservative local safety deadline. What must it do?
options: Stop issuing IDs and surface ownership loss
Continue issuing until a duplicate is detected
Reset its sequence and use the same worker ID
Use the gateway clock to extend its lease locally
explanation: Generation must fail-stop before ownership becomes uncertain. Coordinator consensus does not physically kill an old process, and neither a new clock nor a sequence reset creates a valid allocation.

q: CS14: Two threads call next_id while the millisecond changes. Which synchronization boundary prevents timestamp-reset and sequence races?
options: Only the increment of the sequence field
The full timestamp, rollover and sequence transition
Only the final shift-and-OR expression
Only the background worker-lease renewal
explanation: Timestamp comparison, sequence reset/increment, rollover waiting and state publication must be serialized together. Alternatively callers need genuinely disjoint allocation spaces; an atomic counter alone is insufficient.

q: CS14: A 12-bit sequence permits 4096 IDs per millisecond. What does the resulting 4.096 million IDs/s number represent?
options: A guaranteed throughput of any generator machine
A required minimum arrival rate for valid Snowflake IDs
A sequence-space ceiling before implementation bottlenecks
A global fleet ceiling independent of worker-bit count
explanation: 4096 times 1000 is the representable per-worker rate ceiling. Clock calls, locks, CPU speed, lease checks and rollover waits determine measured throughput; the bit arithmetic is not a benchmark.

q: CS14: A small backward-clock wait finishes, but the generator's lease expired while it waited. What should the next_id call do?
options: Return an ID because wall time has caught up
Return an ID with sequence zero for safety
Move the custom epoch backward and continue
Recheck ownership and reject the issuance
explanation: Clock recovery does not restore ownership. Every wait or pause can cross the lease safety deadline, so issuance must recheck the lease and the granted timestamp range.

q: CS15: With candidate capacity two, the first events are A, A. What should a keyed candidate heap contain?
options: One A entry whose estimated count is updated
Two A entries with their individual event counts
An A entry and an anonymous collision placeholder
No A entry until a distinct second key arrives
explanation: Candidate membership is keyed by event key, not event occurrence. Repeated A updates its existing heap priority and cannot consume a second candidate slot.

q: CS15: A Count-Min Sketch has epsilon=0.001 and has processed 2,000,000 nonnegative events. What is its standard additive error scale for a queried count?
options: 200 events
2,000 events
20,000 events
0.001 events
explanation: The additive upper-error term is epsilon times total events: 0.001 times 2,000,000 equals 2,000. The confidence parameter is separate, and the count bound does not guarantee top-K candidate recall.

q: CS15: Partition 1 has A=100 and X=60; partition 2 has B=100 and X=60. Merging local top-1 misses X=120. Which change restores the exact local-top-K union argument?
options: Round each local count up before selecting its winner
Use the same display cache for both local winners
Route all occurrences of each key to one partition
Publish local top-1 lists twice as frequently
explanation: Whole-key partitioning puts X's complete count under one owner. Exact local top-K union then works under a shared tie order and compatible windows. Arbitrarily split event counts can hide a global winner in every local list.

q: CS15: A worker retains 60 one-minute sketches of 32 MiB each for an approximate last-hour query. How much sketch memory does it need before candidates and metadata?
options: 32 MiB
960 MiB
1 GiB
explanation: 60 times 32 MiB is 1,920 MiB, or 1.875 GiB. Fixed-size per-pane state does not mean a sliding-window implementation has only one pane's memory cost.

q: CS15: A collision caused by B raises retained candidate A's sketch estimate without updating A's heap priority. What does periodic candidate rescoring accomplish?
options: Refreshes retained priorities but cannot recover every omitted key
Makes both sketch counts and candidate recall mathematically exact
Eliminates the need for a unique key-to-heap-index map
Converts a decayed query into an exact sliding-window answer
explanation: Rescoring repairs stale priorities for keys still retained. It cannot discover a missing candidate or remove sketch collisions, so count error and candidate-recall error remain separate.

q: CS15: One worker emits the 12:00-13:00 window and another emits 12:01-13:01. Why is directly merging their winners problematic?
options: A min-heap requires every worker to have equal event volume
The counts answer different time-window questions
CMS arrays cannot represent more than one key at a time
A timestamp forces every event into the same Kafka partition
explanation: The merge must use compatible window IDs, finalization/watermark state and partition ownership. Mismatched intervals do not represent one global frequency query even if the key partitioning is otherwise correct.

q: CS16: A composite Redis score is score*B+(B-1-t). Which condition is necessary for reliable score-first ordering and exact integer storage?
options: B equals the number of active leaderboard users
The reach timestamp uses the full Unix epoch in milliseconds
The tie term is below B and the maximum composite is below 2^53
All scores are positive even when the composite exceeds 2^53
explanation: The tie component must not outweigh a one-point score difference, and the integer composite must fit double precision exactly. A chosen multiplier without explicit bounds establishes neither property.

q: CS16: A projector has stored Dev=125 at version 9. A delayed event carries Dev=95 at version 8. Which action preserves the ranking projection?
options: Apply 95 because it arrived most recently
Add 95 to 125 because events are incremental
Delete Dev until all events arrive in order
Atomically reject version 8 as older than 9
explanation: The projection stores and checks each player's durable update version atomically with the sorted-set change. Arrival order is not authoritative score order, and replayed state updates are not increments.

q: CS16: Under a common snapshot and full tie order, two other shards have 7 and 5 players ahead of Ada; her own shard has 2 ahead. What is Ada's one-based global rank?
explanation: There are 7+5+2=14 players ahead, so Ada is rank 15. Her local rank is only 3. Exact distributed ranking needs compatible snapshots and consistent tie semantics.

q: CS16: Score-range sharding places only 40 players in the highest range. How should an exact top-100 query proceed?
options: Return 40 players because lower ranges cannot enter top-100
Take those 40 and continue through lower ranges for the remaining 60
Duplicate the highest 40 until the response contains 100 entries
Estimate 60 unnamed ranks from the highest shard's histogram
explanation: The highest shard contains the entire top-100 only if it has at least 100 members. Otherwise continue through lower score ranges, respecting the global order and consistent migration/snapshot state.

q: CS16: A score API writes SQL successfully and crashes before updating Redis. Which design makes the missing ranking update recoverable?
options: Issue an extra ZINCRBY whenever the client refreshes its rank
Treat Redis persistence as a replacement for the missing SQL event
Commit the score and an outbox event together, then replay versioned updates
Return an exact rank from whichever store responds first after the crash
explanation: A durable score plus atomic outbox records both the authority and the need to update its projection. A version-aware projector can replay safely after crashes or duplicates; a bare dual-write cannot provide that guarantee.

q: CS16: A season-maximum board receives match M82 with score 125 twice for a player whose prior maximum is 95. What should the second submission do?
options: Increase the score to 250 using the repeated match result
Increase the score to 220 by adding it to the prior maximum
Set the score back to 95 until the match is independently replayed
Return the deduplicated result with the maximum still 125
explanation: The stated score contract is a season maximum, with stable match/player/season dedupe. Replaying the same match does not create another increment or lower an accepted maximum.

q: CS17: Four serving cache nodes are each measured at 200,000 ops/s before headroom. What aggregate throughput does that arithmetic provide?
explanation: Four times 200,000 is 800,000, not millions per second. Replication work, fills, invalidations and utilization headroom can reduce the usable request rate.

q: CS17: Every one of 1M reads/s performs a cache GET. Each node sustains 200k ops/s, but the target is 70% utilization. What is the GET-only serving-node lower bound?
options: 4 nodes
8 nodes
5 nodes
7 nodes
explanation: Each node contributes 140k ops/s at the target utilization. ceil(1,000,000/140,000)=8. Misses still perform GETs; fills and other operations require additional capacity.

q: CS17: Reader R fetches DB version 7, a writer commits version 8 and invalidates, then R fills version 7. Which mitigation addresses this stale-fill race?
options: Delete the cache key only before committing the database update
Increase the value TTL so readers perform fewer misses
Condition the fill on an unchanged per-key generation fence
Move the same unconditional cache fill to a different replica
explanation: A writer advances the generation while invalidating; the older reader's conditional fill then fails. The fence must survive value deletion and not be reused after eviction/restart. Strict freshness still requires addressing the commit-to-invalidation gap.

q: CS17: After a cold restart, 1M distinct-key misses/s reach a database budgeted for 120k reads/s. What should the cache tier do?
options: Forward every miss because single-flight always merges distinct keys
Disable cache admission so the database warms all keys immediately
Increase TTLs for values that have not yet been fetched
Bound database fills, prioritize warming and shed excess optional reads
explanation: Single-flight merges concurrent fills of the same key, not distinct cold keys. Admission control, staged warming and load shedding protect the database from the abrupt loss of cache hits.

q: CS17: A design labels its generic clockwise consistent-hash ring as Redis Cluster. Which correction is accurate?
options: Redis Cluster routes via 16,384 hash slots and slot ownership
Redis Cluster routes every key through one Sentinel ring leader
Redis Cluster uses one virtual node for each cached byte
Redis Cluster requires hash(key) modulo the current node count
explanation: Redis Cluster uses hash slots with explicit ownership/migration. Sentinel handles monitoring and failover for standalone primary-replica groups; neither is the generic ring protocol drawn for a conceptual distributed cache.

q: CS17: A cache sizing exercise needs four nodes for memory but eight for request throughput. Which starting deployment bound is justified?
options: Four nodes, because memory is the cache's only scarce resource
At least eight serving nodes, then add failure and other-operation headroom
Six nodes, because averaging the two estimates balances the resources
Twelve primaries, because independent lower bounds must always be added
explanation: The deployment must satisfy both constraints, so use the larger lower bound rather than their average or automatic sum. Add overhead and replication separately and validate with the intended workload.

q: CS18: At 5,000 jobs/s and 0.2 seconds average service time, what does Little's Law imply before utilization headroom?
options: 1,000 required worker machines regardless of slots per machine
25,000 execution slots regardless of job duration
1,000 busy execution slots, with machines depending on concurrency
5,000 persistent database connections for every worker machine
explanation: Arrival rate times service time is 1,000 concurrent executions. That is a slot count; a machine may host many slots, subject to CPU, memory and I/O requirements.

q: CS18: Job-42 is now leased as attempt 8. Attempt 7 sends a late success ACK. Which database operation is safe?
options: Delete job-42 because any successful attempt completes current ownership
Reset attempts to zero before accepting the late acknowledgement
Extend attempt 8's lease using the old worker's success timestamp
Update only if state, valid lease and attempt token still match 7
explanation: The stale attempt's conditional update affects zero rows. Acknowledging by job ID alone can delete or complete a newer attempt's work, while a token identifies current ownership.

q: CS18: A hierarchical timing wheel has a fixed array of buckets and now tracks ten times as many jobs. What happens to timer storage?
options: Job-entry storage still grows with the number of timers
Total timer storage remains constant because bucket count is fixed
Every extra job is encoded in the bucket index without storage
A durable job row removes the need to store any timer reference
explanation: Bucket metadata can be fixed, but each scheduled timer still requires an entry/reference. Processing a due bucket also costs work proportional to the timers in it.

q: CS18: A recurrence planner advances next_fire and then crashes before inserting the due occurrence. Which design prevents this lost run?
options: Store next_fire only in the planner's memory until the next restart
Insert the unique occurrence and advance next_fire in one transaction
Let every worker independently create the same cron occurrence
Create the next occurrence only after deleting the schedule definition
explanation: Atomically pairing occurrence creation with schedule advancement ensures both persist or neither does. A unique (schedule_id, scheduled_at) identity makes planner replay safe.

q: CS18: A worker's lease expires during an external email send, and a retry sends again. Which identity should the effect sink dedupe?
options: The worker process ID, which changes on reassignment
The attempt number, which intentionally changes for every retry
The stable job or scheduled-occurrence identity
The heartbeat timestamp, which changes during long executions
explanation: All attempts of the same intended effect must share its dedupe identity. Attempt-token checks protect queue ownership, but preventing duplicate email requires dedupe at the effect boundary.

q: CS18: A 02:00 local-time report encounters a DST day with no 02:00. What must the schedule contract specify?
options: That the timing wheel can invent the missing local timestamp
That using UTC storage removes every local-time policy decision
That the worker must run twice to compensate for the missing hour
A timezone and an explicit nonexistent-time/misfire policy
explanation: Persisting UTC instants is useful, but recurring local schedules still need timezone, DST, missed-run and overlap rules. Skipping or shifting a nonexistent local time are policy choices, not accidental implementation behavior.

q: CS19: Alice has 5,000 cents. T30 posts a 3,000-cent debit under a balance lock but does not update the balance row. T31 then checks that row for a 2,500-cent debit. What is missing?
options: Authoritative balance maintenance in the same ledger transaction
An extra display cache with a longer expiration time
A second idempotency key for T30's already accepted debit
An asynchronous notification before releasing the account lock
explanation: Without the transactional balance update, T31 can still read 5,000 and overspend. The lock is useful only if the protected state reflects the posted debit before the next transaction acquires it.

q: CS19: A retry finds a matching durable payment row in PENDING after a possible external charge. What should the API return or do?
options: Return a completed success receipt without checking the posting stage
Return status or resume the existing payment identity
Delete the pending row and create a new provider charge key
Treat row existence as proof that the provider declined the charge
explanation: PENDING proves that an operation exists, not that it completed. Resume/query the same transaction and provider identity, while terminal identical requests replay their stored result.

q: CS19: A client reuses the same tenant/principal/operation idempotency key but changes the amount from 1,000 to 2,000 cents. What is the correct response?
options: Charge the difference and keep the original result body
Treat the larger amount as a harmless network retry
Reject the reuse because the canonical payload differs
Replay the original key into a new transaction with a fresh amount
explanation: Scoped idempotency binds a stable key to a canonical payload. Changed amount, currency or accounts represent a different intent and must not silently reuse the existing payment identity.

q: CS19: Alice and Bob are on different ledger shards. Which design represents a transfer without pretending a saga is an atomic cross-shard commit?
options: Debit Alice on A and credit Bob on B without any clearing entries
Update both cached balances and let reconciliation invent missing history
Declare global balance preservation because each service has a retry loop
Post balanced clearing legs locally and track the transfer in transit
explanation: Alice-to-outgoing-clearing and incoming-clearing-to-Bob are each balanced local postings. A durable transfer links their progress and compensation, but simultaneous cross-shard visibility still requires a stronger transaction protocol.

q: CS19: A provider charge times out after the request was sent. Which next action avoids conflating transport failure with payment outcome?
options: Persist UNKNOWN and query using the same provider payment identity
Persist FAILED and immediately send another charge with a new key
Credit the wallet because a timeout implies the charge probably succeeded
Remove the idempotency record so a later retry starts from a clean state
explanation: The provider may have charged despite the lost response. UNKNOWN requires durable status resolution with the original payment identity; a fresh blind charge can duplicate money movement.

q: CS19: The rate is 2,000 transactions/s on average, two entries per transaction, 200 bytes per entry. What is the approximate daily ledger payload before indexes and replicas?
options: About 346 GB/day
About 69 GB/day
About 17 GB/day
About 1.7 GB/day
explanation: 2,000*86,400*2*200 = 69,120,000,000 bytes, about 69 GB/day. Sustaining the separate 10,000/s peak all day would yield about 346 GB, an upper-bound workload rather than this average.

q: CS20: A stock decrement commits, then the process crashes before creating its reservation record. Which change closes this gap?
options: Create the reservation later using a best-effort notification
Give the stock counter a longer Redis expiration time
Commit the conditional decrement and reservation creation together
Let the payment processor recreate the missing stock reservation
explanation: Stock and its durable ownership record must change in one transaction. Otherwise a retry can decrement again or recovery cannot explain the held unit.

q: CS20: A Redis reservation key expires. Which fact follows without an explicit release protocol?
options: The durable available-stock count has increased exactly once
The payment associated with that reservation definitely failed
Every replica agrees that the unit can immediately be resold
The key disappeared; stock restoration has not been established
explanation: TTL expiration deletes a key; it does not atomically restore stock or resolve payment. A durable conditional expiry transition must restore quantity once and retain enough state for dedupe.

q: CS20: Confirmation and expiry race for one ACTIVE reservation. What should determine which stock transition succeeds?
options: Conditional state transitions against the same authoritative reservation
Which callback reaches the user's browser first
Whichever worker sends more retries to the Redis admission cache
An unconditional increment followed by an unconditional confirmation
explanation: Confirmation while valid and expiry at the deadline compete on the same state. Only a successful ACTIVE transition can confirm or restore stock, so duplicate callbacks do not create two outcomes.

q: CS20: A Redis authority loses acknowledged reservations during asynchronous failover. Which action is compatible with a no-oversell promise?
options: Resume from the older stock count and reconcile after the sale
Stop sales until ownership and acknowledged reservation state are recovered
Reset stock to the original sale quantity because Redis is empty
Treat lost holds as cancelled without checking payments or confirmations
explanation: Lost accepted holds can make old stock appear available again. No-oversell requires a durability/recovery protocol before resuming admissions; after-the-fact reconciliation cannot undo overselling.

q: CS20: R17 expired, another buyer obtained its released unit, and payment P17 later succeeded. What should happen next?
options: Confirm R17 because payment success overrides inventory state
Decrement available stock below zero to honor the original checkout
Try a fresh reservation or complete an idempotent refund
Delete P17's record so the accounting system ignores the charge
explanation: The expired reservation no longer owns stock. Payment success is not an inventory grant; obtain a new hold or reverse the charge through a tracked idempotent refund.

q: CS20: A ticket system has two available seats, but both requests select concert-9/A12. What extra constraint distinguishes this from fungible SKU inventory?
options: A larger aggregate seat counter with the same decrement script
A fixed ordering of email notifications to both buyers
A longer payment timeout for named-seat purchases
Unique active ownership for the specific event-and-seat pair
explanation: Aggregate quantity cannot prevent two buyers from claiming the same named seat. The reservation authority must enforce uniqueness of active/confirmed ownership for (event, seat).

q: CS21: N=3, W=2, R=2 are configured. What does W+R>N prove by itself?
options: Read/write-set intersection when both use the same fixed home replica set
Linearizable operations even with arbitrary stand-in replicas
No concurrent sibling versions can ever be created
A failed write never leaves a visible partial version
explanation: The arithmetic is a set-intersection statement under fixed membership. Retention, resolution, concurrency, failed writes and operation ordering still matter, and sloppy quorums may not intersect at all.

q: CS21: Home replicas are A/B/C. A sloppy write succeeds on A/D, while a read reaches B/C. What result is possible?
options: The read must return the write because 2+2 is greater than 3
The read can return an older version because the successful sets are disjoint
D automatically becomes part of every reader's home replica set
The write cannot have been acknowledged under any sloppy policy
explanation: A/D and B/C do not intersect. W and R were not chosen from the same fixed three-node universe, so the strict-quorum overlap argument does not apply.

q: CS21: Alice reads cart siblings, merges them and adds tea. Which PUT input communicates that the new value supersedes the versions she read?
options: Only the wall-clock time shown by Alice's browser
Only a random request ID unrelated to the read versions
The merged version context returned by the GET
The address of whichever replica answered fastest
explanation: The client returns the observed causal context, and the coordinator advances it for the new write. Omitting context makes a blind update that may be concurrent rather than a descendant of the read versions.

q: CS21: A/B purge a deletion tombstone while offline C still has the old live value. What failure can follow when C rejoins?
options: The old value becomes a valid read-your-writes token
The deleted key is automatically assigned a new global UUID
The tombstone is reconstructed from the key's hash position
The deleted value can be resurrected during repair
explanation: Without the deletion version, an old replica can reintroduce live data. Tombstone retention, repair guarantees and rebootstrap/quarantine rules for long-offline replicas must prevent this.

q: CS21: The next three virtual nodes on a ring all belong to the same physical machine. How should an N=3 replica preference list be formed?
options: Skip repeated owners and choose distinct physical failure domains
Use those three virtual nodes because three positions imply three failures
Count each virtual node twice to increase write durability
Disable repair because co-located replicas already share a disk
explanation: Virtual nodes improve partition balance but are not independent machines. Replica selection must spread across distinct physical owners and the intended failure domains.

q: CS21: In strict mode with home A/B/C and W=2, a writer can reach only A plus non-home D/E. What should it report?
options: Success because any two reachable machines count as strict replicas
No successful strict-quorum acknowledgement under this connectivity
Success if A's wall clock is newer than B and C
Success after updating only the client's cached version vector
explanation: Only one home replica is reachable, so a strict two-home-replica write cannot be acknowledged. Accepting stand-ins is a deliberate sloppy-quorum mode change, not strict behavior.

q: CS22: A view-once paste was atomically claimed, but the connection broke before the API knows what bytes arrived. Which promise can the design enforce?
options: Exactly one human has read and understood the paste
The claimant cannot save or copy any returned bytes
At most one authorized retrieval attempt under the chosen contract
A second claim is safe whenever the server misses the final ACK
explanation: The system can atomically authorize one retrieval attempt, not observe human viewing or reliably infer delivery from a lost response. Resetting consumed state can permit another retrieval.

q: CS22: A private view-once paste is stored in object storage. Which read path preserves the access and consumption rules?
options: Return a permanent public object URL after checking the short key once
Let the CDN serve cached bytes before the metadata authorization lookup
Put the private body in a shared cache keyed only by the short URL
Authorize and claim in metadata, then proxy the private blob with no-store
explanation: The private origin must not be an alternate bypass around ACL, expiry or consumption. Proxying after the authoritative claim avoids handing out a reusable public retrieval URL.

q: CS22: A paste expires at 12:05, but physical blob cleanup runs at 12:10. What should a read at 12:06 do?
options: Reject it using the serving-time expiry check
Serve it because the object still exists until the sweep
Extend expiry automatically to match the cleanup schedule
Consume it once more because expired pastes no longer have metadata
explanation: Access expiry is enforced on the read path using current authoritative metadata/server time. Lifecycle deletion reclaims storage later and is not the access-control mechanism.

q: CS22: Uploading p7/v1 succeeds, but committing its metadata fails. Which cleanup approach is appropriate?
options: Delete every object whose upload timestamp is older than one second
After a grace period, verify no authoritative reference and remove the orphan
Create public metadata automatically for every unreferenced object
Keep every orphan forever because metadata writes cannot be retried
explanation: Two-store creation can leave orphan payloads. A grace period plus authoritative reference check avoids racing a still-completing metadata write, while idempotent cleanup reclaims genuine orphans.

q: CS22: A small internal paste service stores 2-KB text bodies and metadata in one indexed SQL table. Which scaling advice is justified?
options: Move immediately because SQL cannot store multi-kilobyte strings
Replace authorization with unguessable keys before adding more users
Keep the simple baseline until payload or traffic measurements justify splitting
Add a public CDN to every paste regardless of privacy and expiry rules
explanation: SQL text storage is a valid small-scale baseline. Splitting metadata and blobs becomes useful for measured payload/retention/traffic pressure, but adds orphan cleanup and protected-serving complexity.

q: CS22: An ordinary public paste is cached by a CDN and expires in two minutes. What cache constraint is necessary?
options: Use a one-day TTL because public content never needs expiry checks
Ignore metadata expiry until the object-store lifecycle policy executes
Convert every public read into a permanent private signed URL
Ensure cache freshness cannot outlive expiry and handle early deletion
explanation: A CDN must not keep serving beyond the paste's access lifetime. TTL bounded by expiry plus purge or an access gate for early deletion/revocation preserves the serving contract.

q: CS23: O901 contains two shirts at 1,999 cents each, shipping 300 cents and zero tax. What total should its accepted price snapshot store?
options: 4,298 cents
3,998 cents
4,598 cents
2,299 cents
explanation: 2*1,999+300=4,298 cents. Persist the accepted unit prices, quantities, currency and adjustments so retries do not silently recalculate a different payment.

q: CS23: O901's provider call times out after transmission. Which order behavior is consistent with the payment design?
options: Mark FAILED and retry checkout with a new provider identity
Persist PAYMENT_UNKNOWN and reconcile the same P901 payment
Mark CONFIRMED because inventory was reserved before the charge
Archive the order immediately because no response means it is terminal
explanation: Transport timeout does not establish decline. The durable order saga must resolve P901 while handling reservation expiry separately; it must not create a second charge or claim confirmed ownership without evidence.

q: CS23: Browse showed price version 16, but checkout authority returns a higher version-17 price. What should checkout do?
options: Charge the current price silently because browse is availability-first
Use the stale badge as authority to avoid an extra checkout decision
Validate and obtain acceptance for the changed quote before charging
Skip the reservation because a price change invalidates inventory counts
explanation: Stale browse data is a UX tolerance, not permission to change the purchase contract silently. Checkout validates current price/stock and persists the accepted snapshot before the payment intent.

q: CS23: An order has status DELIVERED but an open refund dispute. Which archival decision is appropriate?
options: Delete the hot row because DELIVERED implies immutable history forever
Copy once and route every future order operation directly to a public cache
Ignore the dispute because returns were out of the interview's core scope
Apply an explicit eligibility policy that considers active workflows
explanation: A terminal fulfillment label does not mean no future financial/support changes. Archive eligibility needs retention, legal-hold and open-workflow rules, followed by verified copy and version-safe routing/deletion.

q: CS23: The archive holds order version 8, but a refund updates the hot row to version 9 before deletion. Which action avoids losing the new state?
options: Condition deletion on the copied version and re-evaluate eligibility
Delete by order ID because the archive already has some version
Overwrite version 9 with version 8 so the stores match for cleanup
Send the history reader to whichever copy has fewer fields
explanation: The verified copy is of a specific version. Deletion must fail if the hot version changed; the new workflow/version needs appropriate archival handling and the read path must dedupe and route correctly.

q: CS23: A small shop has varied shirt and TV attributes but modest load. Which initial data model is defensible?
options: One independent database service for every product attribute
Indexed SQL with JSON/category tables and transactional orders
A distributed saga for every product-page read
A cold archive as the sole authority for active checkout state
explanation: Polymorphic attributes do not force a document database or a microservice fleet. SQL JSON/category tables are a reasonable baseline; split services and add specialized indexes when requirements and measurements justify their costs.

q: F1: With KV caching, what is the dense-attention work for one new token as context length t grows, holding model dimensions fixed?
options: O(1), because appending the new cache entry is constant-size
O(log t), because every KV cache is an ANN tree
O(t), because attention still reads the prior context
O(t^3), because all previous projections must be recomputed
explanation: KV reuse avoids recomputing prior keys/values, but new-token dense attention still scans context. Constant-size cache append and linear attention work are different operations.

q: F1: A model uses 128 KiB of KV per token. How much KV does one 4,096-token sequence require before weights and workspace?
options: 128 MiB
256 MiB
4 GiB
512 MiB
explanation: 128 KiB*4,096=524,288 KiB=512 MiB. This depends on the model's layer/KV-head/dimension/precision configuration; it is not a universal per-sequence size.

q: F1: There are 10,000 open chats, 20% actively decoding at 30 output tokens/s. What aggregate decode demand should this active fraction imply?
options: 60,000 output tokens/s
300,000 output tokens/s
2,000 output tokens/s
600,000 output tokens/s
explanation: 10,000*0.2*30=60,000 tokens/s. Open conversation count is not the same as actively decoding sequence count; prefill and memory requirements must still be sized separately.

q: F1: A client disconnects while its request is in a continuous decode batch. What should the serving stack do?
options: Keep decoding to the maximum output length before freeing its pages
Cancel at a safe scheduling boundary and reclaim its KV allocation
Cancel every other sequence because the batch shares one request identity
Move its KV state to a public prompt cache without checking isolation
explanation: Cancellation stops wasted decode work and reclaims per-sequence state without disrupting unrelated sequences. Batch membership and KV allocation must support safe per-request removal.

q: F1: Two users submit the same prompt text under different private conversation histories and permissions. Which response-cache policy is safe?
options: Share the result because exact prompt text proves semantic equivalence
Share the result if embedding similarity exceeds a high threshold
Require matching context, model, permission scope and freshness
Use only the output token count as the distinguishing cache key
explanation: The same text can have different meanings or permitted evidence in different conversations. Cache identity must bind model/adapter, context/system prompt, tenant/authorization and relevant freshness/decoding settings.

q: F1: Generated tokens are streamed directly to clients while a moderation service analyzes a separate copy. What change is needed to enforce pre-delivery output screening?
options: Screen only the input prompt because decode output cannot change its safety
Add another asynchronous analytics topic after the client stream
Skip screening for cached answers because they were generated earlier
Place an output gate before every delivered chunk, including cache hits
explanation: An asynchronous observer cannot prevent already delivered content. A pre-delivery gate must screen streamed/cached output; any necessary buffering becomes part of the TTFT and inter-token latency contract.

q: F2: ANN returns old refund/v7/c2 with score 0.91 and current refund/v8/c2 with score 0.89. What should determine usable evidence?
options: Current-version validity and permission, not similarity alone
Always the higher ANN score regardless of document version
Whichever chunk has more overlapping query words
The old version until physical vector cleanup finishes
explanation: Similarity is not freshness or authorization. The current-version manifest and live permissions reject obsolete/restricted evidence before it enters context, even if its vector similarity is high.

q: F2: A document is revoked but its vector rows will remain indexed for another minute. What should protect a new query during that interval?
options: The future vector-deletion job alone, with no query-path check
A current authoritative permission/tombstone gate before context
A lower ANN top-k so the document is less likely to be retrieved
A citation disclaimer added after the revoked text reaches the model
explanation: Query-time authorization and deletion checks must block revoked evidence while index cleanup lags. Stored ACL metadata is not enough if stale; a disclaimer after context assembly does not undo disclosure.

q: F2: Recall misses the only authorized passage needed for a policy question. What can reranking guarantee?
options: It will reconstruct the missing passage from the query embedding
It will make an unrelated high-scoring passage sufficient evidence
It can reorder available candidates, not recover an absent passage
It will repair the index freshness lag without an ingestion operation
explanation: Reranking operates on the retrieved candidate set. Missing evidence needs another permitted retrieval route or abstention, not confidence inferred from a rerank score.

q: F2: A query has no sufficient current authorized evidence within its budget. Which behavior is preferable?
options: Answer from superseded policy because it has a confident similarity score
Use a restricted document and hide its citation to protect the source
Ask the model to fill the evidence gap without revealing uncertainty
Abstain or request clarification with the evidence limitation stated
explanation: Grounded systems should not substitute fluent unsupported claims for missing evidence. A bounded permitted fallback is reasonable; otherwise abstention protects answer quality and access rules.

q: F2: Of 20 labeled questions, 16 are answerable from authorized documents and retrieval finds evidence for 14. What is evidence recall among answerable questions?
explanation: Evidence recall is 14/16=87.5%, not 14/20. The four unanswerable questions instead test appropriate abstention, and generation/citation quality require separate measurements.

q: F2: A service has 100 million 768-dimensional float32 embeddings. What storage figure describes the vectors alone?
options: About 76.8 GB including replicas and chunk text
About 307.2 GB before index, metadata, text and replicas
About 3.072 GB because ANN compresses every vector automatically
About 614.4 MB because only nearest neighbors are retained
explanation: 100,000,000*768*4 bytes=307.2 billion bytes. An ANN index adds structure and may optionally compress vectors; compression and replication cannot be assumed away.

q: F3: A feed unions 700 ANN, 300 followed and 200 trending candidates into 1,000 distinct items, then ranks 500 after filtering/pruning. Why is this funnel useful?
options: It guarantees the globally optimal ranking over the full catalog
It makes feature fetch unnecessary for the heavy ranking model
It limits expensive scoring while trading off candidate recall
It removes the need to enforce policy on the final list
explanation: Cheap recall and pruning constrain the expensive ranker's work to its latency/compute budget. Relevant items can be missed, so recall and policy still need evaluation rather than an optimality claim.

q: F3: A last-click feature is six minutes old but has a two-minute freshness limit. Which serving behavior is appropriate?
options: Treat the old value as fresh because the feature definition is shared
Replace it with zero and report no missing-data signal
Wait indefinitely for a fresh value even after the feature budget expires
Use a trained stale/missing-feature path and record the fallback
explanation: Freshness is part of the feature contract. Use tested missing indicators or a simpler fallback model, rather than silently changing semantics or violating the request's latency budget.

q: F3: A training row describes an impression at 10:00, and the latest profile includes its resulting click at 10:01. Which join avoids leakage?
options: Use feature versions that were available by the 10:00 prediction time
Use the latest profile because it contains the most complete history
Use any feature event timestamp from the same calendar day
Use the clicked item's current popularity because it is an aggregate
explanation: Training features must reflect information available at serving time, considering both event time and availability time. Including the later response leaks the outcome into the model's inputs.

q: F3: A new user has no interaction history. Which initial feed preserves a useful cold-start path?
options: Refuse to show items until the user has historical clicks
Serve eligible regional/trending items plus bounded onboarding-based exploration
Assign the nearest existing user's private history to the new account
Rank the entire catalog with the largest model to compensate for no features
explanation: A safe nonpersonalized/onboarding fallback creates useful exposure while data accumulates. Cold start should not require behavior that cannot happen without first showing content.

q: F3: The highest scores are I17=0.81 and I18=0.80 from creator X, then I24=0.73 from Y and I31=0.70 from Z. With one item per creator in the top three, what should be served?
explanation: Keep the best item from X, then take the next eligible distinct creators Y and Z. Policy re-ranking can change the raw model-score order while honoring the stated relevance/diversity constraint.

q: F3: An experiment raises CTR but also increases hide/report rates and pushes end-to-end p99 above 200 ms. What is the appropriate launch judgment?
options: Launch automatically because CTR dominates every recommendation objective
Ignore latency because only model inference time counts toward the budget
Remove reports from evaluation because they are sparse negative feedback
Evaluate the primary outcome with safety, quality and latency guardrails
explanation: One engagement metric does not override explicit guardrails. Higher CTR can coexist with worse user experience or unsafe/repetitive content, and the full serving pipeline must meet its latency target.
